items.title: Devagar Que A Vida É Curta
Parallel Commutator
items.note: Valentina Magaletti, João Pais Filipe and Leon Marks make two long pieces of clattering polyrhythm under synth haze. The Quietus made it Album of the Week.
items.source: The Quietus, The Line of Best Fit

items.title: Corps Perdu
items.note: Fofana turns the words of Aimé Césaire and others into sound. It is heavy and quiet at once.
items.source: a closer listen, Fall Music Preview

items.title: Somewhere Between
items.note: The follow-up to On The Inside, with guests including Rosie Lowe and Matt Maltese. Warm, loose and soulful.

items.title: Chinese Benefits
items.note: Louis Johnstone, of Wanda Group, mixes stream of consciousness spoken word, abrasive noise and fractured electronics. Short tracks, odd and prickly.

items.title: Eyes Bright and Low
items.note: Ambient leaning, with a ten minute title track and a guest vocal from Rachael Lavelle. Described as light waves crashing on an autumn shore.
items.source: a closer listen, Fall Music Preview

items.title: Hits Different
items.note: The second album from the Kraków jazz group, after Jazz Report From The Hood. It shifts to a narrator's point of view.

items.title: Lost Meridians
items.note: Music to pause to, inspired by open prairies. One long title piece, and some short ones.
items.source: a closer listen, Fall Music Preview

items.title: Answers
items.note: Fully instrumental, recorded remotely between Wales and Austria. Tape warmed guitar on one side, liquid synth on the other. Lead single is "Lichen Trip".

items.title: Through to Us
items.note: Experimental compositions built on nature recordings, birdsong, synths and a piano passage. The title track runs about eight minutes.

items.title: Live at Keystone Korner
items.note: A posthumous live set from the organist, recorded in 2022. Eight tracks, with long takes on "Lady G" and "Vibrations in Blue".

items.title: Edge Conditions
items.note: Out October 9 on International Anthem. Eleven tracks of electronic music that AllMusic hears as 90s post-rock meeting experimental electro, with Booker Stardrum and Takako Minekawa along. Worth it for the band feel inside the machines.

items.title: Opening
items.note: Reversed acoustic instruments and stretched vocal samples, and it leans on unease through simplicity. Quiet, strange and patient.

items.title: Nightlife
items.note: Western Vinyl. Modular synth with Greg Fox on drums and Matt Bauder on sax and flute, made in late night sessions. Spacious and a bit like a small band playing in a dark room.

items.artist: Lothar Ohlmeier / Isambard Khroustaliov / Rudi Fischerlehner
items.title: Landscapes
items.note: Third album from this Berlin trio on Not Applicable. Bass clarinet, drums and electronics, free improv that nods to musique concrete and punk.

items.title: Testing the Waters
items.note: A long electroacoustic piece in five movements, first made for WDR 3 radio in Cologne in 2023. Field recordings and slow detail.

items.title: Ama Lel Hawa
items.note: Mostly solo oud, rooted in maqam, with three ensemble pieces that open it up gently. Her first solo full length. Warm and close.

items.title: Music Is Invisible (Pentimento Volume Three)
items.note: Out October 2 on Ndeya. Music from his Pentimento Trilogy. Worth a listen for that fourth-world trumpet haze.

items.title: Radical Frame
items.note: Musique concrete mixed with club-ready production. A strange, dense record.

items.title: Phren
items.note: A collaboration between a producer and a guitarist. Listed as ambient and experimental.

items.title: Waters Dance
items.note: Listed as jazz on Bandcamp. I found little else, so this one is a hunch.

items.title: Cyano
items.note: Out on RVNG Intl. Ambient, experimental electronic, from a reliably calm writer.

items.title: LUMINA
items.note: The Italian duo moves electronics to the centre, with synths and club rhythms beside oud, cello and vibraphone.

items.title: AT/DC
items.note: Warm guitar and banjo with reverb and synth. Described as close to Rain Drinkers.

items.title: RUIN: It's Not Just Music
items.note: Ambient, experimental electronic. I could not find more detail than that.

items.title: Friction
items.note: Out on Dragon's Eye Recordings. Field recordings with wordless vocals and a sense of endless space.

items.title: Baby Ghost
items.note: Falsetto voice mixed with bowed double bass, which gives it an otherworldly feel.

items.title: Linda's Head
items.note: Guitar songs that drift and smudge, on Grouper's own label. Quiet, strange and worth the full run.

items.title: Last Light of the Sun
items.note: Ambient, IDM, dub techno and a little drum and bass, with bamboo flute and typewriter in the mix. Soft on top, with real movement underneath.

items.title: Neram Pularumbol
items.note: Kerala drumming, drones and club bass, followed by a second half of remixes. Heavy in places, but it treats tradition as something alive.

items.title: Passing the Cup of Sorrows 1.1
items.note: The first piece from his album due 23 October. Tape-loop ambient, slow and sad.

items.title: Archives
items.note: Homemade instruments and chopped samples, built remotely between rural France and a London boat. The Quietus hears Autechre reworking The Wicker Man. Raw and odd.

items.title: SÖWT
items.note: Tenor saxophone drawing on Moroccan Gnawa tradition, set against blues-rooted jazz. A good one for a long evening.

items.title: Songs for Sad Poets Vol. III
items.note: Drone that breaks into short bursts out of long silence. Dark, patient and well suited to headphones.

items.title: Post Dub Cities
items.note: Austere dub-leaning electronics that sound like empty streets and wear. Cold and spare, in a good way.

items.title: Psychic Video
items.note: A preview from his DJ-Kicks mix, out 16 October. Dark, textured club music.

items.title: Shell and Core
items.note: Arabic-language post-rock and jazz, about lives left unfinished, like abandoned buildings.

items.title: Traces of Light
items.note: A saxophone quartet in quiet, searching post-bop, nine originals. The gentle pick of the week.

items.title: Alive Alone, Alive Together
items.note: Live guitar from four cities, fuzz and blues running through it, with Hamid Drake on drums for four tracks.

items.title: Saints in The Wethouse
items.note: His debut album on XL, industrial rap collapsed into gothic synths and marching percussion, with dancehall guests and real intensity. Quiet moments like the acoustic "The Wind" cut through the chaos and give it weight.

items.title: Extraxxion
items.note: Debut album from Magu's KCR1 project, mixing bass, dub, gqom and changa with Afro-Venezuelan drums. Heavy, strange and physical.

items.title: Dizzy
items.note: Dear's return to Ghostly International, a sleazy, strutting electroclash single. Short, sharp and fun.

items.title: Devagar Que A Vida É Curta
items.note: Her second album, traditional Portuguese folk run through DAW-built electronics at full urgency, with tectonic percussion. A thrilling, defiant record about slowing down to actually live.

items.title: any1 can cook!
items.note: An Edinburgh producer's EP that moves fast between footwork, Jersey club, grime and baile funk without ever settling down. Restless, rough-edged club music.

items.title: Blackcurrant Jam
items.note: Sparse, jacking acid house from London's Mytron, from the Ascorbic EP. Lean and hypnotic, built for a late set.

items.title: Ma Waraa Al-Shaabi / Beyond Shaabi
items.note: Recorded in Iceland, his third solo album mixes high-BPM electronic dabke with slower drones and IDM textures. One foot in Levantine folk tradition, one in something far stranger.

items.title: Chapman's Pool
items.note: Will Dorey's one-man-band suite of breezy, lo-fi AM radio songs on a strong classic funk backbone, with some stranger detours. Easy to love, a little scuffed round the edges.

items.title: Snakes & Ladders
items.note: A surprise album about modern life lulling people into complacency, with jazz-leaning beats from Kenny Segal and others and plenty of gallows humour. billy woods and E L U C I D at their sharpest.

items.title: Warm Ground
items.note: Seven restrained, improvised guitar miniatures in under 18 minutes, with creaky doors and dropped mics worked into the texture. Small, warm and strange in the best way.

items.title: Birth Is Upon Me, Death Is Upon Me
items.note: Belfast trio using the studio as an instrument, threading fiddle and guitar through heavily improvised, electronics-tinged jazz. Inspired by personal loss and their Northern Irish surroundings, it's atmospheric and genuinely moving.

items.title: Songs For Sinners
items.note: His first album in six years, mixing gospel, jazz and Caribbean soundsystem rhythms with 808s. London jazz with a dancefloor pulse, from one of its best drummers.

items.title: Nu Zamrock
items.note: Third album, reimagining 1970s Zambian Zamrock through hip-hop, poetry and soul. Confident and rhythm-forward, rooted in her own family history.

items.title: Late Loop
items.note: First album in five years, built under strict self-imposed rules, with vocals from Alison Skidmore and Elaine Howley threaded through his usual heavy, waterlogged low end. Still unmistakably his own sound.

items.title: Places Remember Events
items.note: upsammy and Piezo's debut as a duo, made across the Netherlands and Italy. Elegant, angular electronica mixing her ambient instincts with his bass and techno leanings, with a nostalgic streak running through it.

items.title: Music for Empty Stadiums
items.note: John Talabot's new ambient alias, a 17 track, 95 minute beatless record made during lockdown. Patient and uneventful in the best way, built for empty rooms rather than dancefloors.

items.title: Burning Song
items.note: Recorded alone at Leipzig's Thomaskirche, her first solo album in two years. Slow moving pipe organ drone that rewards full attention, with more weight and grief in it than usual.
Debut album, described as a rock record with no guitars: live drums and bass colliding with synths and samples, with James Murphy producing one track. Restless and narcotic, built for moving.

items.title: Begin Yr Singing
items.note: A Chicago supergroup's debut, six live-tracked instrumentals with two overdriven guitars and improvised horns. Somewhere between Sonny Sharrock and Crazy Horse, loose and physical.

items.title: Final Circle
items.note: A five track meeting of Skee Mask's dub ambience and North Americans' dreamy Americana guitar work. Understated and warm, good for the long nights coming.

items.title: Passing the Cup of Sorrows
items.note: A return to solo piano for the Disintegration Loops composer, recorded alone and mostly unadorned. Spare and meditative, with more grief in it than usual.

items.title: FUDGE
items.note: His first album since going public with a serious health battle, and it sounds like a man taking his time to get things right. Warm, classic soul songwriting, understated rather than showy.

items.title: Heaven Can Wait
items.note: Her first release on Ghostly International, a euphoric, slightly woozy track about the rush of city life. Short and good, worth the three minutes.

items.title: Sing the Color Blue
items.note: Chicago drummer Mike Reed's genre-blurring quintet, moving between post-bop, chamber music and something closer to indie rock without ever losing the swing.

items.title: Aldehydes and Ketones
items.note: His first solo single in almost five years, slow burning with a heavy low end and textures that feel like they're dissolving as you listen. Genuinely strange in a good way.

items.title: LP1
items.note: Ex GoGo Penguin drummer Rob Turner and keyboardist Liviu Gheorghe's debut as a duo, spiritual jazz run through beat driven electronics. Good for anyone who liked GoGo Penguin but wanted it rougher round the edges.

items.title: theukhasmorefoodbanksthanbranchesofmcdonalds.com
items.note: Built entirely from samples of food bank items, pasta, tinned fruit, toilet roll, as a pointed piece about poverty in Britain. Conceptual in a way that could feel gimmicky but mostly just lands.

items.title: We Never Learn (feat. Kudbeu)
items.note: A restrained, quietly ecstatic deep house cut from one of South Africa's steadiest producers. Good late night driving music.

items.title: It's a Style Sport
items.note: Ishmael Butler's project keeps mutating, this one woozier and more collaged than the last couple of records. Dense and slippery, rewards repeat listens.

items.title: Edge Conditions
items.note: Modular synths woven through acoustic instruments and field recordings into something warm and human, a little Jon Hassell in its spirit. Came out a couple weeks back but too good to leave off.

items.title: No Bad Memories
items.note: Their first album in six years, and it sounds like it. A sun soaked collage of samples and guest vocals, very much in the spirit of Since I Left You.

items.artist: Enrico Rava Fearless Five with Joe Lovano
items.title: Corners
items.note: Rava's quintet with Joe Lovano sitting in, recorded in Rome. Loose and lyrical, with the kind of chemistry you only get from players who've logged this many years together.

items.title: Chinese Benefits
items.note: Louis Johnstone, who also records as Wanda Group, mixing stream of consciousness spoken word with harsh noise and broken electronics. Bleak and bracing.

items.title: Follow The Light
items.note: Her debut, blending dub reggae with vintage psych folk and classic soul, shaped by growing up in a Jamaican household in South Florida. Warm and unhurried.

items.title: Hippies, Thugs and Heroes
items.note: His 20th studio album, and one of his strongest in years. The songwriting leads, the band stays tight behind him, and the guitar work is there without ever showing off.

items.title: Dopamine Chamber
items.note: Fifth album, picked up a five star review this week. Denser and more unsettled than what came before, but still unmistakably them.

items.title: In Time And Spirit
items.note: A London sextet led by guitarist Jean de Talhouët, built around a three part title suite with contrapuntal writing. Unusually optimistic for contemporary jazz.

items.title: Live at the Globe
items.note: Canadian guitar legend Lorne Lofsky and Nigel Price trading lines live in the north of England, recorded last November. Conversational, unhurried guitar jazz.

items.title: Back to The Halcyon
items.note: A joint EP marking five years of IMOGEN's WIGS label. White knuckle rave nostalgia, unapologetically maximalist.

items.title: Chronicles of Gnowt (Vol 2)
items.note: Second in Gnod's new triptych, heavy and repetitive with dub abstraction and spoken word running through the centerpiece track. Technically out October 9th, but too good to leave out.

items.title: Music Is Invisible (Pentimento Volume Three)
items.note: Previously unheard trio recordings of the late Fourth World pioneer, reworking themes from across his catalogue. It completes a trilogy he never lived to finish and it's the closest thing to a lost Hassell album we're going to get.

items.title: Melting Pillars of Snow
items.note: Contrabass recorder, shō, bowed cymbals and tape loops of spoken W.G. Sebald, with Swans' Michael Gira turning up on one track. Dense, slow-building electroacoustic work. Needs a dark room and your full attention.

items.title: Allison de Groot & Rich Ruth
items.note: A bluegrass banjo player and an ambient synth producer from Nashville, out on Western Vinyl. Clawhammer banjo through looping and delay set against pedal steel, strings and field recordings of cicadas. The two sounds never fully merge, which is what makes it work.

items.title: Lumina
items.note: Italian duo mixing drum machines and arpeggiators with oud, cello, xylophone and vibraphone. More club-facing than their earlier records but still unmistakably their own thing, world music that doesn't sound like a pastiche.

items.title: Nearly
items.note: Nathan Jenkins' first solo album in two years, made across London, Toronto and Montreal. Vocal-led electronic pop with L Devine guesting, understated and well-arranged rather than flashy. A grower.

items.title: Ruin: It's Not Just Music
items.note: A hard swerve from her usual modular ambient work into jungle, drum & bass and future garage, most of it past 170 BPM. Still unmistakably her, just with teeth.

items.title: Eugene / Save The World
items.note: Two sides of UK soul from Nao, one tender, one more upbeat. Not a huge event release but a genuinely good pair of songs.

items.title: Last Light of the Sun
items.note: Amsterdam producer hopping between ambient, techno, dub, dream pop and drum & bass across one record without it feeling scattered.

items.title: Archives
items.note: New studio album despite the title, the trio swapping instruments and working remotely across different cities. A collage of postmodern songcraft, warm and a bit woozy rather than clinical.

items.title: All For Free
items.note: A Juno Daily exclusive this week. Dub-inflected downbeat, slow and spacious.

items.title: Snakes & Ladders
items.note: billy woods and ELUCID dropped this as a surprise on Backwoodz, with a different producer on every track. Pitchfork calls it intimate and close-up, with political and technological unease running through small, detailed sound worlds.
items.source: Pitchfork, 9 New Albums You Should Listen to Now

items.artist: Anna Butterss, John Raymond, Ben Lumsdaine
items.title: Beginningless
items.note: Bass, horn and drums improvising live over two days in an LA studio, out on Northern Spy. Pitchfork hears it as spontaneous but grounded, and the trio name Jon Hassell as an influence.
items.source: Pitchfork, 9 New Albums You Should Listen to Now

items.title: Echo
items.note: His first solo album since 2019, about six years in the making and self-released on his own label. Pitchfork says it starts from cloud rap and wanders into pop rock, IDM and trip-hop.
items.source: Pitchfork, 9 New Albums You Should Listen to Now

items.title: Legendary Love
items.note: Her first full album since 2021, written around a two and a half year relationship. Warm production that leans on 80s and 90s R&B, with Nile Rodgers and Raphael Saadiq helping out.
items.source: Pitchfork, 9 New Albums You Should Listen to Now

items.title: Secret Language
items.note: The band's first full-length in 11 years, on Exploding in Sound. Pitchfork says it turns their usual inward-looking style toward parenthood, hobbies and grown-up responsibilities.
items.source: Pitchfork, 9 New Albums You Should Listen to Now

items.title: Trouble Mountain
items.note: Their first album together since 2021's Garbology, out on Rhymesayers. It's built around a ski resort fantasy set in the Poconos, with Blockhead on production.
items.source: Pitchfork, 9 New Albums You Should Listen to Now

items.title: Pirouette
items.note: A longer, more ambitious record than before. Pitchfork describes a pop and EDM base that pulls in emo, twee, ambient and choral music, with Mk.gee producing one track.
items.source: Pitchfork, 9 New Albums You Should Listen to Now

items.title: Year of the Rooster
items.note: The last of their Zodiac Cycle albums and the end of the Grass Can Move Stones trilogy, out on Tankcrimes with a lot of punk and rock guests. I couldn't find it on Spotify yet.
items.source: Pitchfork, 9 New Albums You Should Listen to Now

items.title: Dossier Scriptorium de Toulouse
items.note: The story of the Scriptorium de Toulouse, a type and calligraphy workshop that ran from 1967 to 2005 and trained a generation of French letter makers. Mostly unpublished documents and first-hand accounts, with contributions from nearly twenty type designers and calligraphers. 240 pages, two colour offset, French and English, designed by Juliette Flécheux with Bureau 205 and co-published with ANRT. A good one on how a school's way of teaching shapes the work that comes after it.

items.title: Some Other Book(i)s(h) Logos
items.note: 174 logos from small presses, zine makers, bookshops, book fairs and printers, all redrawn by hand by a third grader called Zaiah Drawing. It's a colouring book too, and the back of each fold gives the name, a short bio and the Instagram handle, so it doubles as a directory of the art book world. Designed by Kristen Mueller, coil bound, risograph and inkjet. Funny, and a sharp test of which marks survive being drawn by a child.

items.title: GraphicDesign.zip
items.note: Nearly a century of Swiss stamp design, looked at through eight lenses: format, shape, sheet layout, material, cropping, symbols, typography and imagery. Braille embossing, fabric stamps and foils turn up along the way. Tiny at 7.4 x 10.5 cm, 96 pages, Wire-O bound. Small screens are your world, and this is all about saying a lot in very little space.

items.title: Dreader Than Dreads: Posters by Fred Voisin
items.note: A folio of concert posters Frédéric Voisin made for reggae shows in Paris: Yellowman, Aswad, Culture, Burning Spear, Dennis Brown. Unbound, 16 pages, full colour, with a short text by Olivier Cachin. Published by le Signe, the national graphic design centre in Chaumont. This week's poster pick, and at $16 an easy one to say yes to.

items.title: PLOP #03: Polish Design Revue
items.note: A slim Polish design magazine asking what graphic design can do beyond selling or looking good. The theme is wrażliwość, roughly sensitivity or openness. Inside: Poster Rex's collective screen printing, Sonia Góral's family imagery, and Podpunkt's safety booklet that went to 16.8 million Polish households. 32 pages. Out in December.
items.by: Marian Misiak, Rene Wawrzkiewicz and Lars Harmsen

items.title: Mag to Mag Journal #2
items.note: The journal of Milan's independent magazine fair, run by the shop Frab's. This issue's theme is "Error", with interviews with MacGuffin's Ernst van der Hoeven, TypeOne's Amber Weaver and the Fukt team, plus a look at the Dutch distributor Idea Books. Big format, 160 pages, designed by Laura Bortolotti. A quick read on where indie magazines are now.

items.title: Fracture: Japanese Graphic Design 1875 to 1975
items.note: Not new (2024), but it fits well after the Japan books from earlier lists. Lynam traces Japanese graphic design from the graphic arts to just before digital, through essays on modernity, empire, gender, commerce and taste. 447 pages, hardback, from Set Margins'.

items.title: Graphic Design Play Book, Second Edition
items.note: Sophie Cure and Aurélien Farina teach type, signage, logos, posters and branding through puzzles: spot the difference, matching, dot to dot. Work by Otl Aicher, Otto Neurath and Gerd Arntz turns up along the way. Light, but handy for warming up a team workshop.

items.title: Meet the Lithographer
items.note: A picture book tour of a lithographer's workshop, from the invention of lithography to how books, posters and magazines get printed now. 40 pages, illustrations in three colours. Made for kids, but a clear, charming explainer at any age. Its sister book, Meet the Typographer, is there too.

items.title: Podpunkt
items.note: Warsaw branding studio behind the City of Warsaw logo, Culture.pl, the Adam Mickiewicz Institute and the Kraków National Museum, with a digital sister studio, Superskrypt, for UX and code. They also designed Poland's national safety guide. Public-facing design at real scale. Follow for identity systems that have to work for everyone.

items.title: Velvetyne Saved My Life
items.note: A book about Velvetyne, the French collective that has released open source typefaces since 2011. It's built around a group interview by Sandra Chamaret, with essays on their key typefaces and a catalogue of more than 70 fonts by almost as many designers. Half reading book, half specimen, and good on what a foundry can be when the fonts are free.

items.title: Zweikommasieben #31
items.note: The Lucerne music magazine turns 15 in print with a 452-page issue shaped like a cigarette packet, 55 x 88 mm. The theme is "Where there is smoke, there is fire": Sylvie Fleury talks with Russell Haswell, there's a piece on the band Kleenex, and an essay on how digital life breaks up our sense of time. Designed by Studio Laurenz Brunner. A format idea worth stealing.

items.title: Revue Faire no. 30 bis: Types of Types, the Typographic Specimen by Lineto
items.note: A short study of how the Swiss foundry Lineto sells its typefaces: books, posters, envelopes, videos, inflatables, even bootleg logos. It includes REALA's 2000 LL Biff specimen, which drew on graffiti. 84 pages, French and English, an expanded reprint from Editions Empire. A specimen is product design, really, and this shows it.

items.title: Bye Bye Binary, No. eụ: Archives typo·graphiques du futur
items.note: The second magazine from the Franco-Belgian collective that designs type for gender inclusive French. This one is about archives: essays, visual research, Clara Balaguer looking back at Filipino Folk Foundry, and two type specimens built from texts by bell hooks, Sara Ahmed and others. Pocket sized, 160 pages, black and white, in French. Worth it even with rusty French, for how type can carry a political idea.

items.title: Yearbook of Type #8: History Edition
items.note: Slanted's survey of type released from 2024 to 2026, this time leaning on history and heritage. Each typeface gets three pages: a specimen spread, then a profile with weights, language support and OpenType features. 528 pages, hardcover with open thread stitching, designed by Samira Niedermayer and Viola Dessin. A handy desk reference when you're choosing type for a product.

items.title: Signs and Artifacts No. 5: CDMX, Mexico City
items.note: Shop signs from Mexico City, photographed and lifted out of their streets so you can really look at the lettering. Collected and designed by Can Can Press and Secret Riso Club, 230 pages, one colour offset, English and Spanish. Sits nicely next to the Showa Modern signs book from last week.
items.by: Can Can Press and Secret Riso Club

items.title: Breakout #2: 100 Posters
items.note: Tamti started making a poster a day on Instagram as a "graphic design gym". Some won awards and brought in clients. This second book collects 100 posters from 2022 to 2025, from commissions to community work, with a foreword by Götz Gramlich. 128 pages, from Slanted. This week's poster pick, and a good case for practice as a habit.

items.title: POSEUTEO POSTER: Contemporary Poster Designs from Korea
items.note: 538 pages of current Korean posters, from work rooted in calligraphy to plain modern type. It's a Victionary survey, so it skims, but it pairs well with Slanted's Seoul issue from last week. Compact and softbound.

items.title: Merch: We Love Our Customers
items.note: Counter-Print's case for merch as a real brand channel, from political badges and oil company road maps to the tote bag. Examples include Hey Studio's identity for Casa ñidro, carried across awning, totes and staff shirts. Light reading, but useful the next time merch turns up as an afterthought on a brief.

items.title: Götz Gramlich, gggrafik
items.note: Gramlich runs gggrafik in Heidelberg, after a spell assisting Niklaus Troxler in Willisau. Bold, often political posters, the Mut zur Wut poster competition he started in 2011, and a stint as president of 100 Beste Plakate. Follow for the posters.

items.title: Letters and Spirit: New Typography, 2025 to 2026
items.note: Takes Tschichold's The New Typography as a starting point and asks what "new typography" means when layout gets handed to algorithms and generative tools. Essays, case studies and visual experiments, with contributions from Radim Peško, Marian Misiak and others. Designed by Noviki, 272 pages, small and black and white. Probably the most relevant book on this list to your day job.

items.title: Alphabettes Soup: Feminist Approaches to Type
items.note: Ten years of Alphabettes, the network of women in type, collected into one book. Key articles from the site, new essays, interviews and a specimen of over 100 typefaces by women and non-binary designers. Designed by Tereza Bettinardi, 384 pages, from Bikini Books. It sits well next to the Popova book and UN/SEEN from earlier lists.

items.title: Alphabet in Motion: How Letters Get Their Shape
items.note: A type history told in 17 pop-ups. One uses projected light for 1960s psychedelic lettering, one explains anti-aliasing, one is a modular puzzle based on Albers' Kombinations-Schrift. A 128-page essay section puts each one in context. Pricey, but it shows how type follows technology better than most textbooks.

items.title: Oh So Pretty: Punk in Print 1976 to 1980
items.note: About 500 items from Toby Mott's punk collection: gig posters, flyers, fanzines and badges, from famous bands to tiny venues and political groups. Rick Poynor writes on it. 512 pages, now £20. This week's poster pick, and a good reminder that cheap and fast can still be great design.

items.title: Isidro Ferrer: About Nothing
items.note: Ferrer is one of Spain's great poster makers, with a sense of humour built out of found objects and odd juxtapositions. This isn't a straight monograph. It's arranged around themes like farce, disorder, wandering and time, mixing well known and lesser known work with his own writing. 224 pages, from Hoaki (2023).

items.title: Slanted #48: Seoul
items.note: Slanted's city issue on Seoul. The team visited fifteen studios and covers graphic design, type, architecture and digital work, plus essays on K-pop, fashion and city life. 224 pages, in English. Seoul's design scene is one of the liveliest anywhere right now, and this is a quick way in.

items.title: BranD #82: Philippe Weisbecker
items.note: The Hong Kong design magazine gives a whole issue to Weisbecker, the French artist who draws everyday objects and machines with "nothing more than a pencil and a line". Biography, a 2023 interview and excerpts from his books, in a chalk coloured card casing. 200 pages, Chinese and English. Quiet, patient work.

items.title: Showa Modern: Signs and Store Designs, 1920s to 30s
items.note: The sister book to the Showa Modern ad book from an earlier list. Shop signs, window displays and street graphics from Japanese cities as Western styles poured in. Pocket sized, 264 pages, Japanese and English. Cheap, and full of lettering ideas.

items.title: NODE Berlin Oslo
items.note: Serge Rompza and Anders Hofgaard's studio, split between Berlin and Oslo since 2003. Exhibition graphics, books and identities, usually built on a strong typographic idea. Their 2026 poster for Seeing Words, Reading Images at the PalaisPopulaire, a show about writing in art, is a good place to start.

items.title: Graphic Design in Japan: Mapping a Generation
items.note: Eighteen Japanese studios and designers born between 1970 and 1990, drawn from about twenty interviews Dimos has done since 2018. It skips the Yokoo and Tanaka history lesson and looks at how this generation works now, across culture and commerce with no hard line between them. Most of the work hasn't been seen much in Europe. 192 pages, from Éditions B42.

items.title: Women's Rights are Human Rights
items.note: International posters on gender inequality, violence and reproductive rights, by dozens of designers and agencies. Resnick introduces it and Steven Heller adds a text. 224 pages, 23 x 30 cm, from Set Margins'. This week's poster pick, and a reminder of what a poster can still do when it has something to say.

items.title: Letterform Frequencies: Exploring the Visual Imprint of Arabic Type
items.note: Nammour runs the Arabic Type Research Unit in Beirut. Here she counts and maps how often letters and their contextual forms repeat in running Arabic text, which behaves nothing like Latin. Part data, part visual experiment, 264 pages with a poster wrap. Pattern finding that changes how you design.

items.title: To design is also getting on a bus, gazing out the window and thinking on the move
items.note: Notes a Barcelona designer wrote on the H6 bus, which became a newsletter, then a book. Impostor syndrome, uncertainty, who gets to decide, and a case against constant digital urgency. Small, 160 pages, from Set Margins'. One to hand to anyone on your team who's running hot.

items.title: Logos of the Venezuelan Minitecas
items.note: Hundreds of logos from Venezuela's minitecas, the small sound systems that played electro, Miami bass and Italo disco from the 70s on. Compiled by Phran, part of Klasse Wrecks' pocket KFAX logo series. 70 pages, palm sized. Pure vernacular identity work, made by people who never called it that.

items.title: Partners #4
items.note: A Tokyo annual about relationships, one question per issue. This one asks "What do you follow?" and opens with butterflies and Tokuko Ushioda's photos of more than 100 fridges. Designed by Julie Peeters, 400 pages in a compact book format. A study in pacing, like her Bill.

items.title: Slanted Experimental Type 4.0
items.note: The fourth round from students at Dortmund, led by Lars Harmsen and Andreas Ruhe. Typefaces built from accidents, imprecision and odd systems, including variable and AI-made fonts. 296 pages. Not all of it will land, but it's a good look at where students are pushing type.

items.title: Jurriaan Schrofer (1926 to 1990)
items.note: Not new (2014), but on Counter-Print's shelf and worth knowing. Schrofer did photobooks, brochures, magazines and typefaces, and spent years on optical effects and perspective in type. 424 pages, designed by Jaap van Triest and Karel Martens, so it pairs well with the Martens books from earlier lists.

items.title: Amphorae: An Incomplete Compendium of Non-Ancient Greek Vessels
items.note: 157 drawings of made-up amphorae, some close to the real thing, some not at all, many carrying hand-lettered lines like "Can I Pet Your Dog?". A tiny 320-page softcover from Hyper Hypo in Athens. Light relief, and a smart riff on decoration as message.

items.title: Fons Hickmann m23
items.note: Hickmann co-founded the Berlin studio in 2001 with Gesine Grotrian-Steinweg. Conceptual posters, books and identity systems, and he has led the 100 Beste Plakate poster association since 2018. He teaches at the Berlin University of the Arts too. Follow for the posters.

items.title: Segments: Atlas of a Data Leak
items.note: Albrecht took a leaked set of over 650,000 audience segments from 93 data brokers and mapped them. These are the boxes people get sorted into by behaviour, mood and even morals. 330 pages, 97 diagrams, set in Monument Grotesk. The closest thing to your day job on this list, and a sobering one.

items.title: Karel Martens: Cloakroom Tickets
items.note: Martens kept a booklet of numbered cloakroom tickets in his studio for years, meaning to print over it one day. He finally did: 50 monoprints, reproduced front and back at actual size. A quieter, odder companion to his 2027 calendar.

items.title: Saâdane Afif: Affiches 2
items.note: The first book given over entirely to Afif's posters, in an expanded edition from Triangle Books in Brussels. Each poster was made for a show or performance and carries its title, date and collaborators, so together they read as an archive of his work. 176 pages, 24 x 32 cm. A good case for the poster as a record, not just an announcement.

items.title: Assume Nothing: On Practice-Based Art, Design and Education
items.note: Projects by 32 recent graduates of the design and art faculty in Bolzano, paired with new essays on teaching. The idea is that not knowing is a working condition, not a failing. Designed by Melani De Luca, 224 pages. Worth a look if you mentor people early in their careers.

items.title: Fine Design: A Studio Guide to Remixing Design, Art, Craft, and Industry
items.note: Twenty years of studio teaching boiled down into essays and workbook-style exercises, about design that sits between art, craft and industry. Foreword by Andrew Blauvelt. It leans towards objects rather than graphics, but the exercises would work with any team.

items.title: Street Report 7: Naptime
items.note: Singapore is often called one of the most sleep-deprived countries in the world. Zohri watched people napping in public, on commutes, at lunch and between shifts, and turned it into explanatory drawings and short texts. A small 144-page paperback. Gentle, funny, and a nice bit of observational information design.

items.title: The National Grid #9
items.note: A graphic design journal from Aotearoa New Zealand, "occasionally looking elsewhere". Edited and designed by Luke Wood, Katie Kerr and Matthew Galloway, 112 pages, co-published with GLORIA Books. A way into a design scene that rarely reaches London.
items.by: Luke Wood, Katie Kerr and Matthew Galloway

items.title: Tools #6: To Blow
items.note: A Paris annual about making, this time on air and breath. Objects made from balloons, a history of inflatable buildings, crystal glassblowing at Saint-Louis, and an essay on breathlessness and bad air. Art directed by Twice studio, 248 pages, French and English. Calm, well paced pages.

items.title: Tinted #1
items.note: A new non-profit annual from Copenhagen that keeps AI-generated content out. Issue one, The Illusion of Hierarchy, is about the gap between what people do and who they are: six interviews, a cover story on veins, an essay on armour. Edited and art directed by Ida Yndal, openbound, 216 pages.

items.title: Daan Rietbergen
items.note: Utrecht designer who worked at Studio Dumbar and came away with a love of grids and systems. His heavy letterforms turn up on posters and as painted murals, including his Nespor typeface on walls in Amsterdam, Utrecht and Eindhoven. A clear line back to Crouwel, with more swagger. Follow for the posters and the walls.

items.title: Volumes: Design Reviewed Remixed Revealed
items.note: Thirty-odd texts from 25 years of writing about graphic design, with four new pieces and fresh afterwords on the old ones. Sections on teaching, on music and album covers, and some short fiction. Liner notes by Rudy VanderLans of Emigre. Good to argue with.

items.title: How Many Female Type Designers Do You Know?
items.note: Part history, part interviews, part specimen. Popova talks to 14 people including Zuzana Licko, Louise Fili and Indra Kupferschmid, then shows typefaces drawn by women. Small hardback, nicely made. A good companion to UN/SEEN.

items.title: Translator #4
items.note: A London quarterly of journalism translated into English from around the world. This issue covers Icelandic fishing, Vietnamese markets and a Serbian mining fight. Big format, art directed by Sofia Azcona, and it was first designed at magCulture. Words first, but the pages are well built.

items.title: Sorties #1
items.note: A first issue about how images of women get made and who they are made for. Rich and poor images sit side by side on purpose. Display type by Selina Bernet, edition of 500, printed in Latvia. Small, pointed, and nicely odd.

items.title: A Book on Zines: New Aesthetics in Zine Design
items.note: 304 pages on zines now, with interviews with artists, designers, publishers and curators. It is a survey, so it skims, but it is a quick way to find people worth following.

items.title: Flower Stamps
items.note: Hundreds of postage stamps from different eras and countries, all flowers and plants. Tiny pieces of state graphic design, each one doing national identity in a few square centimetres. Lovely for colour and for print texture.

items.title: Only You Can Complete Me
items.note: Japanese dekotora trucks: chrome, neon and hand-painted panels on working lorries. Mutrel did the fieldwork herself in car parks and garages, and the book is bilingual French and Japanese. Vernacular identity at full volume.

items.title: Mascot: Mascots in Contemporary Graphic Design
items.note: Counter-Print's survey of brand characters from over 30 studios, split into people, animals, and food and drink. Useful if you have ever had to defend a mascot in a review. Light reading, plenty of ideas.

items.title: I Got Something to Say: Poster Inventory, 2013 to 2021
items.note: Every poster Draw Down made for book fairs, talks and workshops over eight years. One colour, Swiss bound, pocket sized, with short essays from Ian Lynam, Somnath Bhatt and others. A small map of the art book world, told through event posters.

items.title: baldinger•vu-huu
items.note: André Baldinger and Toan Vu-Huu's Paris studio, going since 2008. Type, identities, signage and a lot of very good posters, including this year's for the Chaumont book fair. They teach in Paris, Nancy and Zurich too.

items.title: ECAL: A Typographic Atlas
items.note: 536 pages of type drawn by ECAL students over ten years. Over 400 graduates from 30+ countries, Latin to kanji. A specimen book that doubles as a map of where type is right now.

items.title: UN/SEEN: Women in Graphic Design up to the Bauhaus
items.note: Eisele and Naegele dig up the women who did book, poster, type and packaging design between 1865 and 1919. Foreword by Ellen Lupton. 422 pages, lenticular foil cover. A proper correction to the canon.

items.title: Experimental Jetset: Statement and Counter-Statement 2
items.note: The Amsterdam trio's second volume. 656 pages in a pocket-sized brick, with essays from Lucy Sante and Greil Marcus. Modernism with a post-punk streak. You'll probably read it more than look at it.

items.title: Bill #6
items.note: A magazine with no words. Archive photographs, paper stocks changing as you go, and a mirrored card so you end up in the sequence yourself. Pure pacing and edit.

items.title: Bruno Munari: Fantasy
items.note: Munari's 1977 book on invention and imagination, in English for the first time. Annotated by Jeffrey Schnapp. Small, playful, and a good companion to Design as Art.

items.title: Identity: Chermayeff & Geismar & Haviv
items.note: Sixty years of the firm behind the NBC peacock, the Chase octagon and the Mobil O. Now in a compact edition from Standards Manual. The logo book to own if you only own one.

items.title: What Is Post-Branding?
items.note: Jason Grant of Brisbane activist studio Inkahoots, with Oliver Vodeb. Part essay, part satirical brand manual. A sharp pocketbook for anyone who sells brand work and wants to argue with it.

items.title: Showa Modern: Ad Designs, 1920s to 30s
items.note: Over 200 Japanese ads from the Taisho and early Showa years. Posters, flyers, matchbox labels, packaging. Cheap, dense, and full of colour ideas.

items.title: Studio Feixen
items.note: Felix Pfäffli's Lucerne studio. From 2010 to 2015 he made every poster for the Südpol venue, riso printed, with near total freedom. Now type and animation too. The feed alone is worth it.

items.title: Against Coffee Table Books
items.note: Davide Tolfo and Federico Antonini on everything around books: formats, shelves, collecting, and why we buy more than we read. It started as six essays for Laguna~B's online magazine. Small, one colour, and a nice antidote to the big glossy stuff.

items.title: Logo In Real Life
items.note: What happens to logos once they leave the brand guidelines. Memes, bootlegs, protest signs, fashion. Galluzzo treats the logo as an open work that the public keeps rewriting, which is a useful thing to remember in any identity review.

items.title: Ninety-Nine Graphic Design Workshops: The Way We Attend to Things
items.note: Over a hundred contributors including Ellen Lupton, Johanna Drucker and Erik Kessels. Each workshop is an exercise in paying attention, no kit needed. Good for running team sessions, or just for yourself on a slow Sunday.

items.title: Publishing as Method: Ways of Working Together in Asia
items.note: Seoul collective mediabus interviewed more than thirty small publishers, designers and artists from East Asia to the Middle East. The design follows the argument: black and white on recycled paper, with the stock colour changing every 32 pages. The cover is set in Kedai-Kedai Merdeka by Huruf.

items.title: Library of Artistic Print on Demand
items.note: Artists using Lulu, Blurb and Kindle Direct Publishing to make books. It's honest about the catch: the freedom depends on the platforms' rules. Relevant if you think about tools, templates and who really sets the constraints.

items.title: MacGuffin #16: The Mirror
items.note: The Amsterdam magazine about the life of things, this time mirrors. Gym selfies, a Norwegian town that bounces winter sun into its square, Sottsass's Ultrafragola. Designed by Sandra Kassenaar and still one of the best-paced magazines around.

items.title: The Unimportance of Form and Other Arguments
items.note: Morrison's early writing from 1984 to 2002, including his RCA thesis and the 1991 essay that gives the book its title. Sharp and often funny. The most direct link to your day job on this list.

items.title: Poster Cult
items.note: Kühne prints huge posters in the Swiss Alps on 1960s presses, mixing hot-metal type with laser-cut plates. The book opens with "The poster world is in crisis" and then spends 160 pages arguing otherwise. The follow-up to True Print.

items.title: Design Reviewed
items.note: Matt Lamont's archive of more than 10,000 posters, magazines and bits of print, shared on Instagram. It is turning into a 400-page book with Unit Editions, due summer 2027. Follow for the feed. Back it if you want the book.

items.title: Huruf
items.note: A Kuala Lumpur type collective founded by Sueh Li. They draw from hawker signs, night markets and temple lettering across Malay, Chinese, Tamil and Jawi. A good corrective to Latin-only type thinking.
